job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Below is a text-based issue list for counsel, not a conclusion that any particular operation would be lawful. **Section 2(1)(B)’s risk-based catchall could defeat many apparent threshold exclusions, and an exemption from this bill would not override other applicable law.** I cannot guarantee every possible issue without reviewing the surrounding statutory framework.

### Definition and scope

1. **§§ 2(1)(B), 6 — Undefined “Secretary.”** The bill never identifies the Secretary empowered to determine which additional activities constitute commercial deep seabed mining. Section 6 expressly names the Secretary of State, while section 4 assigns duties to NOAA, leaving the decisionmaker for the catchall uncertain.

2. **§ 2(1)(A) — Per-vessel rather than aggregate threshold.** The definition measures recovery “by a single vessel,” without aggregating an operator’s fleet, affiliated companies, or coordinated operations. Multiple vessels individually below the threshold could escape subparagraph (A), although subparagraph (B) could potentially reach them.

3. **§ 2(1)(A) — Exact tonnage boundary.** Recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons per year, or less, does not satisfy the “more than” threshold. This excludes some commercially significant activity from subparagraph (A), subject to the catchall.

4. **§ 2(1)(A) — Exact depth boundary.** Recovery at exactly 200 meters or shallower falls outside subparagraph (A). The bill specifies neither a depth-measurement method nor how to treat operations crossing the boundary.

5. **§ 2(1)(A) — Undefined annual accounting period.** “Per year” could mean calendar year, rolling twelve-month period, or operating year. The text also does not explain how to treat partial years or whether projected annual recovery can trigger the prohibition before actual recovery exceeds the threshold.

6. **§§ 2(1)(A), 5 — Unclear timing of a threshold-based violation.** The bill does not say whether crossing 10,000 tons makes earlier recovery days unlawful, or whether liability begins only upon crossing the threshold. That uncertainty directly affects daily civil penalties and fair notice.

7. **§ 2(1)(A) — Undefined tonnage measurement.** The text does not specify wet versus dry weight, gross recovered material versus mineral content, or the treatment of sediment, waste, and material returned to the seabed. Different methods could materially change whether an operation crosses the threshold.

8. **§ 2(1)(A) — Unclear meaning of “recovery.”** The bill does not identify whether recovery occurs upon seabed collection, lifting material into the water column, bringing it aboard, or landing it ashore. That omission affects both threshold calculations and which conduct is prohibited.

9. **§ 2(1)(A) — Vessel attribution and non-vessel systems.** Recovery through multiple collection and support vessels, fixed installations, or seabed equipment is not expressly allocated to a particular vessel. Operations without an identifiable recovering vessel present a textual gap under subparagraph (A), though not necessarily under subparagraph (B).

10. **§ 2(1)(A) — Uncertain resource coverage.** “Other mineral resources” is undefined, and “from the seabed” leaves questions about subsurface extraction and materials such as mineral-bearing fluids. The wording also does not expressly resolve whether different resource types count together toward the tonnage threshold.

11. **§ 2(1) — “Commercial” is not an independent requirement.** The definition does not require sale, profit, or commercial intent. Consequently, qualifying scientific or demonstration recovery could be prohibited unless exempted, while profitable operations below the numerical thresholds might fall outside subparagraph (A).

12. **§ 2(1)(B) — Open-ended risk comparison.** “Comparable” risks lack a specified benchmark, assessment method, probability, severity, geographic scale, or time horizon. Subparagraph (A) itself encompasses widely differing operations, making the comparator uncertain and potentially supporting fair-notice or arbitrary-application challenges.

13. **§ 2(1)(B) — Catchall potentially extends beyond mining.** “Any activity” is not expressly limited to mineral recovery, commercial activity, vessels, or depths greater than 200 meters. A broad interpretation could encompass other ecosystem-disturbing activities, creating substantial uncertainty about the prohibition’s outer limits.

14. **§ 2(1)(B) — No specified determination procedure.** The bill does not require regulations, published designations, advance notice, or a particular process for making risk determinations. Generally applicable administrative-law requirements may supply safeguards, but the text leaves uncertainty about when a determination becomes binding and on whom.

15. **§ 2(2) — Incomplete coverage of individuals abroad.** “U.S. person” includes citizens but does not expressly include lawful permanent residents or noncitizen U.S. nationals. Such individuals operating outside the United States are not expressly covered on that status alone.

16. **§ 2(2) — Incomplete coverage of business forms and jurisdictions.** The definition expressly covers only corporations organized under the laws of a “State,” omitting LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other organizational forms. It also leaves uncertain the treatment of federally chartered entities and entities organized in the District of Columbia or U.S. territories.

17. **§§ 2(2), 3(a) — No express foreign-affiliate attribution.** Foreign-incorporated subsidiaries do not become U.S. persons merely through U.S. ownership, and the bill includes no control-based or consolidated-enterprise rule. U.S. participants may nevertheless face liability for their own conduct or under otherwise applicable legal doctrines.

18. **§ 3(a) — Geographic reach is underspecified.** “In the United States” is undefined, and the bill does not expressly address the territorial sea, exclusive economic zone, outer continental shelf, or conduct aboard U.S.-flagged vessels abroad. Those areas have different jurisdictional statuses and cannot simply be treated as interchangeable.

19. **§ 3(a) — Uncertain coverage of supporting conduct.** “Engage in” is undefined, with no express treatment of financing, directing contractors, transporting recovered minerals, processing, or purchasing. The bill also lacks express attempt and anti-circumvention provisions, although general criminal complicity or conspiracy law may still apply.

### Exceptions

20. **§ 3(b) — Broad grandfathering through exploration licenses.** The exception protects “mining” under a pre-enactment exploration license without an express volume cap, phaseout, or limitation to previously conducted activity. Whether it protects commercial recovery depends importantly on what the underlying license actually authorizes; possession of an exploration license alone does not establish that protection.

21. **§ 3(b) — Unspecified qualifying licensing regime.** The bill does not identify the issuer, statutory authority, or jurisdiction of a qualifying “exploration license.” That creates uncertainty about whether foreign or international authorizations qualify, rather than only licenses issued under U.S. law.

22. **§ 3(b) — Renewals, amendments, and transfers unresolved.** The exception does not address whether a pre-enactment license retains its status after renewal, transfer, area expansion, or modification. These events could produce disputes over whether later mining remains under the original license or a new authorization.

23. **§ 3(b) — No express license-status or compliance conditions.** The exception does not expressly require a license to remain valid, in good standing, or in compliance with its conditions. “Conducted under” may imply those requirements, but relying on implication invites disputes over expired, suspended, or noncompliant authorizations.

24. **§ 3(c) — Undefined environmental-assessment purpose.** The exception contains no definition, volume limit, duration limit, or requirement that extraction be reasonably necessary for the assessment. Substantial recovery could therefore be claimed as assessment activity, with no stated boundary separating legitimate testing from commercial production.

25. **§ 3(c) — Mixed-purpose activities unresolved.** The bill does not say whether environmental assessment must be the sole, primary, or merely one purpose of an activity. It also does not prohibit selling recovered material, leaving uncertainty about assessments that generate commercial revenue.

26. **§ 3(c) — No exception-verification mechanism.** No advance approval, independent review, assessment protocol, or assessment-specific recordkeeping is required. The bill also does not expressly allocate the burden of establishing either section 3 exception, leaving that question to applicable legal rules.

### Registry and reporting

27. **§§ 2(3), 4 — Registry coverage does not match prohibition coverage.** Vessels of exactly 5,000 gross tons or less are excluded from registration regardless of recovery volume, while larger recovery-equipped vessels must register even if their activities are lawful or exempt. Small vessels can therefore conduct prohibited activity without triggering this bill’s reporting system.

28. **§ 2(3) — Vessel eligibility is ambiguous.** The text specifies neither the applicable gross-tonnage measurement convention nor when a vessel counts as “equipped” for recovery. Modular equipment, temporary installations, and support vessels create additional classification questions.

29. **§ 4(a) — No express jurisdictional limit on registration.** “Each covered vessel” is not limited by flag, location, ownership, or U.S. connection. Read literally, the provision purports to cover foreign fleets worldwide, but it supplies no corresponding jurisdictional or enforcement framework.

30. **§ 4 — Undefined operator and missing filing mechanics.** The bill does not identify the responsible operator where ownership, chartering, and technical operation are divided. It also omits an initial registration deadline, registration-update requirements, and quarterly report due dates.

31. **§ 4(b) — Reporting duty depends on registration.** Reports are required from “[e]ach registered operator,” not every operator required to register. An operator that fails to register plainly implicates section 4(a), but the wording creates an argument that its separate reporting duty never attached.

32. **§ 4(b) — Reports need not contain compliance-critical information.** A report need only “describ[e]” recovery activities, without specified tonnage, depth, coordinates, dates, measurement methods, or claimed exceptions. Operator certification is not paired with required independent verification or supporting records.

33. **§§ 4–5 — No express penalties for registry violations.** Section 5 penalizes violations of section 3, not failures to register or report under section 4. Other remedies or generally applicable false-statement laws may apply, but this Act supplies no tailored penalty for nonregistration, nonfiling, or inaccurate reporting.

### Enforcement and effective dates

34. **§§ 3–5 — Incomplete enforcement machinery.** NOAA receives filings, but the bill does not designate a lead prohibition-enforcement agency or expressly provide inspection, audit, subpoena, or civil-penalty assessment procedures. Existing federal authority may fill some gaps, so these omissions do not by themselves make the prohibition unenforceable.

35. **§ 5(a) — Daily penalty calculation is unclear.** The text does not explain whether multiple vessels, locations, or distinct operations generate separate daily violations for the same person. Nor does it specify how a continuing operation is counted on days with no physical recovery.

36. **§§ 2(1)(B), 5(b) — Criminal notice and willfulness problems.** Criminal liability may depend on an unspecified Secretary’s risk determination, yet the text does not clarify the knowledge required regarding that determination or the underlying thresholds. “Willfully” provides a culpability requirement, but uncertainty about its application could complicate prosecutions.

37. **§§ 5(a), 8 — Conflicting commencement language.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while section 8 delays the Act’s effectiveness for 180 days. The stronger harmonizing reading may be that no section 3 violation exists before effectiveness, but the conflicting language invites disputes and fair-notice objections.

38. **§§ 3(b), 8 — Different grandfathering and operative dates.** Licenses issued during the 180-day implementation period do not qualify for the pre-enactment exception. This creates a transition problem for newly licensed activity, rather than an additional grandfathering route.

### International agreement and duration

39. **§ 6 — Negotiation obligation and deadline are ambiguous.** “Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” does not clearly specify whether negotiations must begin, reach a particular stage, or conclude by that date. No counterparties, progress report, or consequence for failure are specified.

40. **§ 6 — International equivalence and domestic implementation unresolved.** “Prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3” does not explain whether an agreement must reproduce the definitions, exceptions, or eventual termination of the domestic prohibition. Seeking an agreement does not itself bind foreign operators or supply any necessary domestic implementing authority.

41. **§ 7(a) — Required report is not commissioned.** The bill conditions the early-termination mechanism on a National Academies report but does not direct preparation, assign a commissioning agency, provide a deadline, or authorize funding specifically for it. Existing authority or outside funding might supply a report, but the bill itself does not ensure one.

42. **§ 7(a) — Undefined “serious harm” standard.** There is no specified ecological baseline, acceptable risk level, geographic scale, or time horizon for determining whether mining can occur “without serious harm.” It is also unclear whether the finding concerns all commercial deep seabed mining or only particular technologies, sites, or operating conditions.

43. **§ 7(a) — Termination instrument is procedurally underspecified.** “Finds by joint resolution” does not expressly say “enacts a joint resolution,” or define what it means for Congress to act “on” the report. A legally operative joint resolution ordinarily requires presidential signature or a veto override; the wording should not imply that congressional passage alone suffices.

44. **§ 7(a)–(b) — Sunset overrides the apparent safety condition.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress makes the required finding, but subsection (b) ends the entire Act after ten years regardless. Read together, the finding is an early-exit mechanism, not a condition that must be satisfied before mining can resume under this Act.

45. **§§ 7(b), 8 — Operative duration is shorter than ten years.** The sunset runs from enactment, while effectiveness begins 180 days later. Consequently, the prohibition operates for approximately nine and a half years, absent earlier termination.

46. **§ 7 — Different termination routes leave different obligations.** An early congressional finding ends the section 3 prohibition but does not expressly end registration and reporting under section 4. The ten-year sunset, in contrast, terminates the entire Act, producing materially different post-prohibition obligations.

47. **§ 7(b) — No express wind-down or savings provisions.** The sunset does not address pending investigations, accrued penalties, prosecutions, or outstanding reports. The federal general saving statute may preserve accrued liabilities, so expiration should not be assumed to erase past violations.
